"I get paid a very handsome salary, no doubt about it, but you know, I've got expenses and a future for my kids and my family, too. " In a stroke of luck, Chaffetz was one of the few freshmen members of Congress to have the chance at an office with a window when he drew number six out of 55 in the office lottery. His office in the Longworth House Building comes with a half-bathroom, a closet that fits a cot, and what he calls his "breakfast nook" where he stores Fig Newtons, granola bars and mixed nuts.  Watch more on the thrifty congressman » . The building also has a gym with a shower room, where Chaffetz starts his day about 5:45 each morning. "My home is in Utah. My wife and kids are there," he said. "I'm here to work." Cutting out travel to and from the office allows Chaffetz more time to serve his constituents and return more of their e-mail and phone calls, he said. The savings are certainly a plus for the congressman, who has three children to provide for, car payments and a mortgage to pay. But Chaffetz said his decision had a larger meaning. "We are now $10 trillion in debt. $10 trillion. Those are expenses that have to be paid at some point," he said. If he can tighten his belt in these tough economic times, Chaffetz said, Congress should be able to as well. "Our country has to learn to do more with less," he added. Although he is a relatively unknown freshman in the House, word of Chaffetz's sleeping arrangement is spreading. Republican Rep. Judy Biggert of Illinois, whose office is adjacent to Chaffetz's, said he isn't the first to sleep in his office, and he won't be the last. "This is a job that you have to have, really, two homes. One in your district where you're there on the weekends and then one here during the week, and it's expensive," Rep. Biggert said. "I'm really glad we have a neighbor here to make sure that the neighborhood is safe at night when we're not here," she joked, adding that Chaffetz is actually projecting the right image of the Republican Party by being a "fiscal conservative." Chaffetz said he is finally getting used to sleeping on his not-so-comfortable cot, but that doesn't mean he rests easy at night. "My biggest challenge is what goes on in the hallway at night," Chaffetz said. "There's this cleaning machine that comes down the hall at night. And it's got that obnoxious beep, beep, beep." Despite the din, Chaffetz has no plans to search for another form of housing -- unless his back gives out. "I've got to keep my back in check, but so far, so good," Chaffetz joked. "But look, our troops are sleeping on a lot worse than this."

WASHINGTON (CNN) — At a time of economic turmoil, most Americans are watching their spending carefully, but one freshman congressman is taking cost-cutting to a new level.

Newly elected Rep. Jason Chaffetz, R-Utah, has opted not to rent an apartment in Washington. Instead, he sleeps each night on a cot in his office—one that folds up and fits into a closet.

“I will save $1,500 a month doing this,” Chaffetz said. “I get paid a very handsome salary, no doubt about it, but you know, I’ve got expenses and a future for my kids and my family, too.”

In a stroke of luck, Chaffetz was one of the few freshman members of Congress to secure an office with a window, after drawing number six out of 55 in the office lottery. His office in the Longworth House Office Building includes a half-bathroom, a closet large enough to hold a cot, and what he calls his “breakfast nook,” where he stores Fig Newtons, granola bars, and mixed nuts.

The building also has a gym with a shower room, where Chaffetz begins his day at about 5:45 each morning.

“My home is in Utah. My wife and kids are there,” he said. “I’m here to work.”

Chaffetz said that eliminating the commute to and from the office gives him more time to serve his constituents and respond to more of their emails and phone calls. The savings are also a clear benefit for the congressman, who has three children to support, car payments, and a mortgage.

But Chaffetz said his decision carries a broader message.

“We are now $10 trillion in debt. $10 trillion. Those are expenses that have to be paid at some point,” he said.

If he can tighten his belt in difficult economic times, Chaffetz said, Congress should be able to do the same.

“Our country has to learn to do more with less,” he added.

Although he is a relatively unknown freshman in the House, word of Chaffetz’s sleeping arrangement is spreading. Republican Rep. Judy Biggert of Illinois, whose office is adjacent to Chaffetz’s, said he is not the first member to sleep in his office, and he will not be the last.

“This is a job that you have to have, really, two homes. One in your district where you’re there on the weekends and then one here during the week, and it’s expensive,” Biggert said.

“I’m really glad we have a neighbor here to make sure that the neighborhood is safe at night when we’re not here,” she joked, adding that Chaffetz is projecting the right image of the Republican Party by being a “fiscal conservative.”

Chaffetz said he is finally becoming accustomed to sleeping on his less-than-comfortable cot, though that does not mean he rests easily at night.

“My biggest challenge is what goes on in the hallway at night,” Chaffetz said. “There’s this cleaning machine that comes down the hall at night. And it’s got that obnoxious beep, beep, beep.”

Despite the noise, Chaffetz has no plans to look for other housing—unless his back gives out.

“I’ve got to keep my back in check, but so far, so good,” Chaffetz joked. “But look, our troops are sleeping on a lot worse than this.”

WASHINGTON (CNN) — With the economy in distress, many Americans are watching their spending carefully, but one newly elected member of Congress has taken thriftiness even further.

Rep. Jason Chaffetz, a Republican from Utah, has chosen not to lease an apartment in Washington. Instead, he sleeps each night on a cot that folds up and fits inside a closet in his congressional office.

“This will save me $1,500 a month,” Chaffetz said. “I’m paid a very generous salary, there’s no question about that, but I also have expenses, and I have to think about my children and my family’s future.”

Chaffetz had some good fortune when office assignments were chosen. In the lottery for freshman lawmakers, he drew number six out of 55, giving him one of the rare chances among new members to get an office with a window.

His space in the Longworth House Office Building includes a small half-bathroom, a closet large enough for his cot, and an area he refers to as his “breakfast nook,” where he keeps Fig Newtons, granola bars and mixed nuts.

The building also includes a gym and shower facilities, where Chaffetz begins his mornings at around 5:45.

“My home is in Utah. My wife and children are there,” he said. “I’m here to work.”

By eliminating a commute between an apartment and his office, Chaffetz said he has more time to serve the people he represents, including answering more of their emails and phone calls.

The money saved is also helpful, he said, since he has three children, car payments and a mortgage. But Chaffetz said the choice is about more than personal finances.

“We are now $10 trillion in debt. $10 trillion,” he said. “Those are costs that eventually have to be paid.”

According to Chaffetz, if he can reduce his own expenses during difficult economic times, Congress should be able to do the same.

“Our country has to learn how to accomplish more while spending less,” he said.

Though Chaffetz is still a little-known first-term House member, news of his office sleeping arrangement has begun to circulate.

Rep. Judy Biggert, an Illinois Republican whose office is next to his, said Chaffetz is not the first member of Congress to sleep at work, and he will not be the last.

“This is the kind of job where you really need two residences — one back in your district for weekends and another here during the week — and that costs a lot,” Biggert said.

Jokingly, she added, “I’m very happy we have a neighbor here to keep the area safe at night when the rest of us are gone.”

Biggert also said Chaffetz is sending the right message for the Republican Party by acting as a “fiscal conservative.”

Chaffetz said he is gradually adjusting to sleeping on his less-than-comfortable cot, though that does not mean his nights are peaceful.

“The hardest part is what happens out in the hallway after hours,” he said. “There’s a cleaning machine that comes through at night, and it makes this awful beep, beep, beep sound.”

Even with the noise, Chaffetz said he does not intend to look for other housing — unless his back can no longer handle it.

“I have to make sure my back holds up, but up to now, it’s been fine,” he joked. “But honestly, our troops are sleeping in much worse conditions than this.”

**CAPITOL HILL — A freshman lawmaker is drawing attention not for flashy fundraisers or a high-profile office, but for an unusually frugal approach to life in Washington.**

The new member of Congress, who has quickly become known among colleagues and staff as one of the most budget-conscious lawmakers on the Hill, says he is trying to practice the same fiscal restraint he wants to see from the federal government.

Rather than rent an expensive apartment near the Capitol, the congressman has been using the House gym showers and keeping basic supplies in his congressional office. Staffers say his office shelves are stocked with practical items: granola bars, instant oatmeal, peanut butter, crackers, and other snacks meant to get him through long voting days and late-night negotiations.

In an interview, the freshman lawmaker said the routine is not about political theater, but about priorities.

> “Families across this country are being asked to do more with less,” he said. “Congress should be willing to do the same.”

The comment has quickly become something of a personal slogan, repeated by the lawmaker in committee hearings, hallway interviews, and conversations with constituents.

### A Frugal Image in an Expensive City

Washington, D.C., is routinely ranked among the most expensive cities in the country, and members of Congress are required to maintain some form of presence both in the capital and back home in their districts. While the congressional salary is far above the national median, lawmakers often point to the costs of dual housing, travel, and district obligations.

This freshman member, however, argues that those realities should not separate elected officials from the financial pressures facing ordinary Americans.

He has told colleagues that the office snack stash helps him avoid frequent restaurant meals, while the use of House gym facilities allows him to keep a grueling schedule without adding more expenses.

The lawmaker’s office says he is not seeking special treatment and is following House rules regarding use of congressional facilities.

### Symbolism or Substance?

The congressman’s approach has earned praise from fiscal conservatives, who say it sends a message at a time of record federal spending and growing concern over deficits.

Supporters argue that his personal habits match his political message: cutting waste, reducing unnecessary spending, and forcing federal agencies to justify their budgets.

One ally described the freshman member as “the kind of person who reads receipts, not just budget summaries.”

Critics, however, say the focus on personal thrift risks becoming a distraction from the scale of the federal budget. They argue that skipping takeout or showering at the gym does not translate automatically into meaningful policy.

“Personal frugality can be admirable,” one budget analyst said, “but governing is about trade-offs measured in billions and trillions of dollars. The question is whether that attitude turns into serious legislation.”

### A Message for Congress

The lawmaker says that is exactly the point. He has signaled support for tighter oversight of federal programs, more aggressive audits, and efforts to claw back unspent funds from previous spending packages.

He has also called for Congress to examine its own operations, including office budgets, travel expenses, and procurement practices.

> “If we’re going to ask agencies to justify every dollar, we should be willing to justify ours,” he said. “Taxpayers deserve a government that treats their money like it matters.”

For now, the freshman congressman’s lifestyle has become part of his political brand: early mornings, long votes, a desk drawer full of snacks, and a message aimed squarely at Washington’s spending culture.

Whether that image becomes a passing Capitol Hill curiosity or the foundation for a broader legislative agenda remains to be seen. But in a city known for power lunches and high-dollar receptions, one new member is betting that thrift can still make headlines.

Some sleep in their offices to reduce costs, though the practice has periodically sparked debate over whether congressional offices should double as living quarters.

For Chaffetz, the arrangement fits neatly into a broader conservative message: government should spend less, borrow less and show more respect for taxpayer dollars. At a moment when Congress is debating bailouts, stimulus spending and the size of the federal budget, his office cot has become a small but vivid prop in a larger argument over fiscal responsibility.

Critics may see the gesture as symbolic, even theatrical. But Chaffetz says symbolism matters — especially in a city where, in his view, overspending has become routine.

His savings alone will not make a dent in the federal deficit. But the congressman’s point is that culture matters. If lawmakers expect families and businesses to tighten their belts during hard times, he says, Washington should be willing to do the same.
